items.title: Does Notation Matter? MusicXML Tokenisation for Symbolic Music Generation and Understanding
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34247v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Symbolic music representations encode musical content at varying levels of completeness, from performance-oriented formats such as MIDI to fully notated scores such as MusicXML. Yet the impact of this representational richness on deep learning models remains poorly understood. While tokenisation has been extensively studied for MIDI, score-based formats have received considerably less attention, and MusicXML in particular remains largely unexplored despite being the de-facto standard for score interchange. In this paper, we introduce the first general-purpose tokenisation framework for MusicXML, and conduct a systematic empirical study to determine whether notational richness confers a measurable advantage for deep learning on symbolic music. We train 26 autoregressive and masked language models, comparing MusicXML tokenisation against MIDI and ABC-based representations, probing the effect of different tokenisation strategies within MusicXML, and testing whether music-grammar-aware tokenisation outperforms treating scores as plain text. We evaluate music understanding tasks using linear probing across composer classification, difficulty estimation, and accompaniment suggestion, and generative tasks using objective statistical metrics and a human pairwise preference study. Our results show that MusicXML-tokenised models outperform MIDI and text-based counterparts on understanding and generative tasks.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.34281v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized Artificial Intelligence (AI) by their extraordinary capabilities, like contextual understanding, few-shot/zero-shot learning, code generation, ability to reason and problem-solving. Recent studies have shown immense work on LLMs. Yet, there is limited work on the thorough taxonomy of LLMs. This study would showcase a detailed classification of LLMs, starting with the earlier models like BERT and leading to LLMs like GPT, Gemini, Claude and Grok. We would delve into topics like datasets used to train LLMs, computational power used during training, their hardware specifications, architecture and parameters. Further, we would also look at the limitations, computational challenges and open problems as well. This study would primarily focus on the timeline of LLMs, signifying their growth over the period. Findings reveal a clear pattern: models that optimize the ratio between architectural complexity and data quality exhibit stronger reasoning stability and better alignment, without proportionally increasing the computational load. This desired balance between scaling and sustainability is the defining characteristic of the current generation of AI.

items.title: Controlled Block Proximal Linearized Method for Nonconvex and Nonsmooth Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34390v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider multiblock nonconvex and nonsmooth optimization without assuming bounded iterates or coercivity of the original objective. We propose the Controlled Block Proximal Linearized (CBPL) method, which incorporates a control potential into block updates while retaining the original objective, variables, and constraints. Under explicit control design conditions and the KL property, the control yields boundedness, finite length, whole-sequence convergence of the original variables, and convergence of objective values. At the limit, one limiting subgradient of the original objective vanishes on all effective comparison directions. We apply CBPL to graph-regularized nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF), CP decomposition, and independent-core matrix tri-factorization (NMTF) with $\ell_0$ norm sparsity constraints. We characterize their reconstruction-preserving scale degeneracies, proving that scale criticality is equivalent to graph collapse and that full criticality forces such collapse. Explicit controls provide compact sublevel sets and a uniform positive lower bound on graph action, including with an independent Tucker core, while retaining genuine reconstruction-changing directions. Each block admits an explicit projection and a computable safe step parameter. For ordinary NMF and CP models, whole-sequence convergence to a full critical point follows. Experiments with direct safe updates demonstrate convergence, sustained graph action, and controlled factor and core scales.

items.title: From GPU to TPU with Coding Agents: What Works, What Fails, and What It Costs?
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34422v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A coding agent can migrate a machine learning workload, report success, and still change how the model trains. Rising compute costs, limited accelerator capacity, and vendor dependence are pushing organizations toward alternatives to graphics processing units (GPUs); a key question is whether agent-generated migrations to tensor processing units (TPUs) can be trusted and at what cost. We build a dataset of 148 PyTorch ML research projects and use Claude Code to migrate ten of them from NVIDIA GPUs to Google Cloud TPUs. We independently assess whether each migration runs, preserves numerical behavior, executes on the intended hardware, maintains the project's goal, and delivers acceptable performance. We also examine failures, human effort, and costs. Eight projects meet our project-goal criterion, and migrations require 2.4 human interventions on average. Of 70 execution attempts, 53 fail (76%), and 26 of these failures (49%) raise no error. The most frequent cause is repeated compilation and other execution inefficiencies, while interactions with third-party libraries can silently change the computation: in one four-chip migration, the agent reports success despite a change in gradient clipping that reduces accuracy from 86.53% to 84.89%. Execution costs vary widely: in one workload, TorchTPU, a PyTorch execution backend for TPUs, trains 1.86 times faster and 25% cheaper per run than the GPU. For practitioners, these findings motivate independent reference runs, verification under the intended hardware configuration, and workload-specific acceptance and stopping criteria that account for both computational and human costs.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.34433v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We analyze stochastic mirror descent for minimizing a convex objective expressed as an expectation under the stationary distribution of a Markov chain, using noisy subgradient observations along a single sample path. Through Poisson's equation, we decompose the Markovian noise and control its contribution under regularity and moment conditions that allow the stochastic subgradients and the Poisson solution to be unbounded across the state space. We establish an $O(T^{-1/2})$ bound on the expected suboptimality gap of the weighted-average iterate for an appropriately chosen step size. The analysis does not require aperiodicity or convergence of the chain's marginal distributions to stationarity. For irreducible finite-state chains, we verify the required conditions on the Poisson solution and derive explicit bounds that quantify the effect of periodicity. For irreducible countable-state chains, we verify the required regularity and moment conditions under a geometric Lyapunov drift condition and suitable growth bounds on the stochastic subgradients.

items.title: End-to-End Neural Modeling of EM Response and Design Performance for Free-Form RFIC Passives
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34462v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Passive matching networks are critical components in radio-frequency integrated circuits (RFICs), but their design is bottlenecked by expensive finite-difference-based electromagnetic (EM) simulation. We propose an end-to-end neural framework for free-form RFIC passives that predicts both EM response and downstream design performance under varying frequency and circuit contexts, combining a frequency-conditioned neural simulator with a circuit-conditioned neural solver. To improve design performance prediction, the simulator outputs a neural EM response consisting of both the explicit EM response and a complementary response, together with a dependence regularizer that encourages the two responses to capture orthogonal information. To evaluate the proposed framework, we construct a large-scale dataset of free-form passive layouts, synthesized from both expert-designed contours and random paths. Our 21M-parameter model achieves high accuracy across a broad frequency range, circuit contexts and passive matching settings, with $R^2>0.98$ for almost all targets, while providing orders-of-magnitude faster evaluation than traditional EM simulation. items.summary: arXiv:2610.34466v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Achieving safety in autonomous driving through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) is a critical yet challenging task due to non-stationarity, partial observability, and the need for effective coordination among agents. Although earlier cooperative MARL methods have aimed to improve coordination by sharing encoded state observations, we find these strategies are insufficient in safety-critical scenarios. To address this gap, we present IntNet, a novel MARL framework that enhances safety by incorporating the transmission of vehicle intent and adaptive communication scheduling into a unified end-to-end learning paradigm, jointly optimising all components for safe coordination. Central to our approach is an observation prediction module that enables agents to forecast subsequent policy outputs, which they can then share across a vehicle-to-vehicle network. Our model-free architecture employs a Graph Attention Network to process incoming messages and a scheduler component to dynamically optimise the communication graph for bandwidth efficiency. We compare IntNet against state-of-the-art communicative MARL methods in complex urban environments with both autonomous and human-operated vehicles, achieving improved coordination, lower collision rates, and reducing communication efforts by up to 60\%. Through extensive experiments, we assess the framework's learning efficiency, scalability, and the balance between information sharing and bandwidth usage for collision-free trajectories.

items.title: Intrinsic Gradient Barriers in Pushforward Deep Generative Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34484v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Broad classes of deep generative models (DGMs) operate by learning to map a simple source distribution, such as a standard Gaussian, to a complex high-dimensional target distribution. Despite their success, DGMs often empirically struggle to accurately represent distributions with heavy tails or well-separated modes. In this work, we show that these difficulties reflect intrinsic properties of the underlying transport problem rather than particular neural network architectures or training procedures. We establish quantitative lower bounds on the gradients and Jacobians of pushforward mappings that transport log-concave source distributions to such targets. For heavy-tailed target distributions, the required gradient magnitude grows as the target develops increasingly large moments. For multimodal target distributions, the low-probability regions between well-separated modes similarly force large gradients in the transport map. We discuss how such large derivatives relate to trade-offs between expressivity and numerical stability. Our results hold under substantially weaker regularity conditions than previous analyses and remain stable under perturbations of the target distribution. Finally, we show that these obstructions can be mitigated when the goal is approximation of a given density rather than generative modeling. Specifically, we propose simple classes of bijective reparametrizations that can alleviate the difficult geometric structure and reduce the gradient burden placed on the learned generative map. Numerical experiments support our theoretical analysis.

items.title: Wave Is All You Need: A Quantum Language Model Based on Fully Connected Quantum Boltzmann Machine
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34492v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work proposes a self-attention mechanism based on the fully connected quantum Boltzmann machine (FC-QBM), and further constructs a fully connected quantum Boltzmann machine language model (FC-QBM-LM) using the mechanism as the core engine. By performing unitary evolution on semantic quantum states, the mechanism implicitly implements positional encoding and self-attention computation, eliminating the need to decompose continuous semantic streams into discrete matrices for explicit matrix multiplication, with the measurement results naturally satisfying the normalization condition. Specifically, this work rigorously derives the computational principle of the self-attention mechanism based on FC-QBM, and demonstrates that this mechanism is mathematically equivalent to the classical self-attention mechanism. The mathematical principles governing the training and generation of FC-QBM-LM are thoroughly derived, and the two corresponding algorithms are subsequently developed. An 8-qubit FC-QBM-LM is finally constructed and trained on the corpus of Tang poetry. Under the 8-qubit setting, the quantum layer implements the entire positional encoding and self-attention computation pipeline with only 44 parameters. In the noiseless scenario, the model exhibits favorable convergence. Furthermore, the quantum circuit proposed in this work, which terminates with Y-axis rotation gates, achieves better convergence than the counterpart terminating with X-axis rotation gates. Under the small-sample regime and across eight distinct noise intensity levels, the model demonstrates strong noise robustness, retaining over 99% of its noiseless convergence performance. Experiments on five-character quatrain generation reveal that the model preliminarily exhibits three core capabilities: associative and divergent thinking, content generation across imagery and human-aligned word ordering.

The problem is formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP), solved efficiently via a proposed Lagrangian Relaxation (LR) algorithm, and benchmarked against the NP-hard optimal solution. items.title: Joint Independence Testing for Latent Position Random Graphs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34544v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Kernel techniques are among the most powerful methods in data science and statistics. One of the key properties of kernels contributing to their numerous successful applications is that the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space is expressive enough to encode probability distributions without loss of information or to capture the joint independence of $M\ge 2$ random variables, under mild conditions. Computationally, these measures (i) rely on the so-called Gram matrix which contains the pairwise similarity of sample points, and (ii) converge at a rate $O \left(n^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right)$, where $n$ denotes the sample size. We focus on measuring the independence of latent position random graphs (LPRGs), a model widely-applied for instance in neuroscience, sociology, and epidemiology. In LPRGs a latent representation is associated to each node. The similarity of these representations (meant via a kernel) determines whether two nodes are connected, making the Gram matrices only implicitly observable and the estimation challenging. Despite the fundamental importance of quantifying the independence of $M$ LPRGs, very little is known about the solution of this problem; existing techniques are restricted to $M=2$ components and only guarantee consistency without rates. In this work, (i) we define an independence measure called graph Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion (GHSIC) for $M\ge 2$ LPRGs, (ii) we prove that it can be estimated at a rate $\tilde{O}\left(n^{-\frac{1}{3}}\right)$ relying on spectral decomposition of adjacency matrices, (iii) without the need to choose kernels and their hyperparameters. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed GHSIC estimator both on synthetic examples and in the analysis of brain functional connectivity subnetworks in natural language perception.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.34550v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Foundation models provide powerful representations for unstructured data, such as text and images, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) makes their adaptation to downstream tasks increasingly practical. For neural estimators that lack a tractable sampling distribution, resampling-based procedures offer a flexible route to statistical inference, but they often require hundreds of model fits, making them computationally prohibitive at foundation-model scale. We introduce HIFI, a two-stage fine-tuning framework for statistical inference on parameters such as conditional means. Stage 1 adapts a foundation model once on a larger sample, capturing the complex structure of the data and controlling estimation bias through a single fit. Stage 2 applies a resampling inference procedure to a smaller independent sample, concurrently fitting multiple lightweight PEFT estimators to the residual to quantify estimation variability without relearning the full task. HIFI accommodates a broad class of resampling procedures, including ensemble subsampling and the nonparametric bootstrap. Across vision and text experiments, HIFI scales to pretrained models ranging from tens of millions to more than ten billion parameters while providing accurate point estimates and well-calibrated confidence intervals across diverse architectures, and reduces training compute by up to 91.9% relative to direct resampling. An application to gene-expression inference illustrates the practical value of the framework for uncertainty-aware scientific inference.

items.title: Dream to Assist: Intent-Conditioned World Models for Shared Vehicle Control
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34650v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Assistive agents in shared-control settings face a dual challenge: acting proactively to align with the human's intentions while remaining legible enough for the human to comprehend and fluently respond in real time. We present Dream2Assist, a model-based reinforcement learning framework for tightly-coupled shared decision making that addresses both sides of this challenge. Our approach extends a recurrent state-space world model with intent inference, enabling an assistive policy trained via fictitious co-play to anticipate and support discrete human objectives without overriding human agency. Beyond the computational framework, we describe the full deployment pipeline needed to translate a world-model-based policy into a safe, human-centered system in a resource-efficient way. Crucially, we address the sim-to-real-human gap via policy down-selection and reward restructuring within an iterative human-machine interface design. We validate the framework through three human-subjects studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment spanning two qualitatively distinct domains: high-speed racing (N=30) and urban driving with richer intent structure (N=10). Our results demonstrate that intent conditioning yields measurable improvements in torque alignment and collision rate. We surface key design insights and practices for deploying learning-based assistive agents in safety-critical, real-time human-robot teaming.

items.title: Pro-Active Inference
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34681v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Estimating a population mean is fundamental across scientific applications, but observing every outcome can be prohibitively expensive. Often, covariates and machine learning (ML) predictions are available for the full population, even when only a small subset of outcomes can be observed. How can we leverage this information to proactively select observations to label, update ML predictions as labels arrive, and construct statistically valid confidence intervals? We develop a general, without-replacement formulation of Pro-Active Inference (PAI), extending our earlier with-replacement approach and building on Active Statistical Inference. Rather than making fixed-order label-skip decisions, PAI proactively selects which observation to label next from the remaining covariate pool while accommodating online ML updates. We establish PAI's finite-sample unbiasedness and asymptotic validity, develop an improved finite-sample variance estimator, and extend PAI to superpopulation inference without Bonferroni corrections or $\alpha$-splitting. We characterize PAI's potential efficiency gains over Batch Active Inference in a quasi-oracle setting, highlighting the role of prediction-residual imbalance. Across eight diverse datasets, PAI achieves greater sampling efficiency than Sequential Active Inference in the vast majority of tested settings with near-nominal statistical coverage, using the same ML predictor and uncertainty score. However, comparisons with simpler baselines such as Prediction-Powered Inference and uniform sampling, as well as the closely related Prediction-Powered Active Testing, reveal when additional adaptivity helps or hurts statistical efficiency. Through interpretable, theory-motivated diagnostics and frozen-ML ablations, we investigate when and why PAI gains or loses efficiency, highlighting the initial residual-estimation problem and subsequent online learning dynamics.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.34685v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language-Only Vision-Language Model Selection (LOVM) aims to identify the Vision-Language Model (VLM) with the highest zero-shot accuracy on a target task using only textual information. We revisit the existing LOVM evaluation protocol and argue that ranking metrics, such as top-5 recall and Kendall's rank correlation, do not directly assess the performance of the selected model. We therefore adopt simple regret (SR), defined as the performance gap between the best and selected models, and introduce Outlier-Robust Normalized Regret (ORNR) to account for the varying performance ranges across tasks while reducing sensitivity to outliers. Building on this revised evaluation protocol, we propose Target-Conditioned Expected Source Regret (TC-ESR), a training-free method that selects the model with the lowest similarity-weighted mean regret across source tasks. Across 22 target tasks and 43 VLMs, TC-ESR achieves the lowest mean SR and ORNR among all compared methods. Separately, we identify two sources of target performance leakage in the prior ranking-based evaluation protocol and provide corrections that remove both.

items.title: Machine Learning Applications in the Solar Interior and Atmosphere
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34687v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The solar interior and atmosphere constitute a strongly coupled, multiscale dynamical system defined by continuous temporal evolution. Predicting the state of this system requires modeling physical interactions that span disparate spatial and temporal scales, constrained by heterogeneous and sparse data. This chapter formalizes the Sun within the mathematical framework of dynamical systems theory, defining a global state vector ($\vec{S}$) governed by thermodynamical, kinetic, and magnetic properties. Because solar observations represent projected, multi-modal, and partially observable measurements ($\vec{O}[\vec{S}]$) of this hidden state, pure physics-based deduction is fundamentally constrained. We present a unifying thesis: the primary role of machine learning in heliophysics is to act as a structured family of mathematical operators---specifically Inference ($\mathcal{I}$), Emulation ($\mathcal{E}$), Propagation ($\mathcal{P}$), and Control ($\mathcal{C}$)---that reconstruct, simulate, and couple this global state vector across disparate physical layers. By framing the vast, multi-disciplinary literature within this unified state-space taxonomy, we demonstrate how data-driven techniques bridge observational gaps to resolve hidden multiscale couplings and dramatically accelerate the simulation of non-linear processes, establishing a rigorous pathway to predict the global evolution of the Sun.

items.title: Intrinsic Information Rates of Summaries in Simulation-Based Inference
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34703v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Simulation-based inference often encodes observations $Y$ into a fixed-dimensional summary $S$, with the posterior conditioning only on $S$. While exact preservation often requires infinite information, any such summary imposes a finite information budget on inference which is rarely an explicit choice or measurement. In this paper, we make the budget explicit by modeling the summary as a lossy channel from $Y$ to $S$, and ask two questions: how large must the budget be, and how best is it spent? First, we show for parametric models that this budget, measured by the mutual information $I(Y;S)$, grows unboundedly as the posterior concentrates, even when fixed-dimensional sufficient statistics exist. More generally, the required budget is set by the distribution of the random posterior, and we bound it from above by quantizing posteriors and from below by converses that weight each posterior state by its probability. Second, we show that a finite budget is best spent stochastically. Under a common-support condition on the simulator, covering the continuous observation spaces typical of simulators, a deterministic summary necessarily loses something: a stochastic summary achieves \emph{strictly} lower distortion than every deterministic summary and every time-shared mixture of deterministic summaries at every positive budget too small for exact preservation. Motivated by these results, we insert a binary bottleneck into neural posterior estimators, measure each trained summary's rate, and compare summaries at matched rate. Across four simulator benchmarks and several encoder families, stochastic bottlenecks achieve favorable rate--loss tradeoffs, and architecture rankings change at different information budgets.

items.title: Discovering Topics from Linear Autoencoders
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34739v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Linear recommenders and topic models are similar in that they implicitly learn from co-occurrences of items. However, there has been little study of how these two model families are related. In this work, we show that, under a latent-factor model of the user-item interactions, the latent topics can be discovered from the weight matrix of a closed-form linear autoencoder. These topics provide a basis for interpreting the recommendations, and can be obtained directly from the trained recommender without additional training. Building on our analysis, we further propose novel item and user normalizations that prevent popular items and very active users from dominating the topics. Our experiments on six public datasets demonstrate that our method achieves significantly higher topic quality than every dedicated topic model and matches or exceeds the best linear autoencoder on all six datasets, while its recommendation performance is competitive with the best tuned recommender.

items.title: Interpretable Brain Age Prediction Using White Matter Fiber Orientation Distributions with Rotation-Equivariant Deep Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34825v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion MRI (dMRI) provides information about white matter microstructure that can support brain age prediction. However, many existing prediction models use diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) scalar metrics that omit orientation information. Deep learning is increasingly used for brain age prediction, but conventional CNNs do not explicitly respect the geometric structure of orientation-dependent features. We present an interpretable brain age prediction framework that combines white matter fiber orientation distributions (WM-FODs) with an SE(3) (Special Euclidean group in 3 dimensions) equivariant CNN. The network operates directly on spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients of the FOD, preserving their transformation properties under rotation. Evaluation in 692 participants aged 36-90 years from the Human Connectome Project Aging dataset showed that the combined framework outperformed the evaluated DTI-based models and conventional CNNs. Averaging predictions from five cross-validation models yielded a mean absolute error of 3.54 years and Pearson's correlation of 0.958. Our results indicated that the performance advantage depended on combining WM-FODs with equivariant processing. Prediction accuracy was highest at a maximum SH order of Lmax = 2 and declined at higher orders. Tract-level occlusion, where each segmented tract was masked in turn, revealed age-dependent patterns of model sensitivity, with importance peaks in frontal projection pathways at 36-44 years, the fornix at 45-54 years, the callosal isthmus at 55-64 years, the middle cerebellar peduncle at 65-74 years, and the callosal genu at 75-90 years. These findings support rotation-equivariant processing of WM-FODs for accurate brain age prediction with anatomically interpretable model sensitivity.

items.title: The Noise-Transmission Burden of Diffusion Network: Why Image Prediction Can Outperform Noise Prediction
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34834v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Clean-image prediction ($x$-prediction) and noise prediction yield equivalent population-optimal denoisers, yet can perform very differently in finite diffusion networks. For noisy input $Y_t$ with noise standard deviation $\sigma_t$, a noise predictor $f_{\varepsilon,t}$ induces the clean-image estimate $\widehat X_1=Y_t-\sigma_t f_{\varepsilon,t}(Y_t)$. This reveals a noise-transmission burden: the predictor must preserve information needed to cancel the input corruption. Under Gaussian corruption of $d$-dimensional data, a linear input bottleneck of rank $r<d$ imposes a denoising-error floor $\sigma_t^2(d-r)$ even with unrestricted downstream computation, while the corresponding optimal risk for image prediction remains bounded. EDM attenuates this bottleneck contribution at high noise; exact preconditioning cancels it at every noise level. Without an input bottleneck, assuming exact affine recovery of the noisy patch from the model representation, we characterize how the covariance spectrum of corrections beyond linear denoising determines the width required above the patch dimension. ImageNet experiments with JiT show that measured denoising losses reflect the predicted bottleneck floor and its attenuation or cancellation through preconditioning. Further widening yields larger relative denoising gains at low noise, where corrections beyond linear denoising spread across more directions, consistent with our spectral characterization of the required model width. Together, these results provide a denoising-based account of practical generation-quality gaps across prediction targets, preconditioning choices, and model widths.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.34904v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pretrained Earth observation models may reduce the effort needed to map surface water, but their value depends on the alternative against which they are compared. items.title: Attack logics, not outputs: Concept-based Property Attacks for Shortcut Elimination in Neural Networks
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34923v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep neural networks (NNs) for computer vision are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, such that minuscule malicious changes to inputs may induce unintuitive outputs. One key approach to verify and mitigate such robustness issues is to falsify expected output behavior, which enables local robustness guarantees and adversarial training. Due to the black-box nature of NNs, current attacks only falsify a class of the final output, such as flipping from $\text{stop_sign}$ to $\neg \text{stop_sign}$. In this work we argue that robustness analysis should focus more generally on logical inconsistencies in concept-level reasoning rather than solely on output misclassification. We formalize this perspective through concept-based properties, i.e., constraints over human-interpretable concepts such as $\text{red} \land \text{octogonal} \implies \text{stop_sign}$ and study the falsification of such properties as a principled form of adversarial attack. Furthermore, an implementation of concept-based properties on already trained NNs is proposed using techniques from concept-based explainable artificial intelligence (C-XAI). For that we formally prove that attacks on concept-based properties are expected to have a reduced search space compared to simple class falsification, whilst arguably be more aligned with intuitive robustness targets. The practical effectiveness of our approach for logically informed adversarial training is shown in an empirical study across multiple models and datasets, including both vision and a security-relevant code processing task. Our results demonstrate that concept-level falsification generalizes classical adversarial attacks: Retraining on our novel attacks maintains robustness gains as compared to classical adversarial retraining whilst better eliminating semantic biases.

In the first stage, FTANet classifies sounds into five coarse-grained categories covering 25 fine-grained classes. In the second stage, samples are routed to the corresponding category-specific classifiers for fine-grained recognition. On a self-constructed dataset, FTANet achieves 95.45% coarse-grained accuracy with only 0.2004M parameters. On UrbanSound8K, it achieves 79.24% mean accuracy and 80.37% mean F1-score in ten-fold evaluation, outperforming compared convolutional models. Field tests on the Tianjin Online Acoustic Environment Monitoring Platform yield 87.94% coarse-grained accuracy and 97.21% conditional fine-grained accuracy for natural sounds correctly routed to C2. The complete hierarchical model achieves 87.18% overall accuracy and 87.40% weighted-average F1-score, demonstrating its feasibility for urban environmental noise monitoring.

items.title: Intellectual Property Protection of Hyperdimensional Computing Classifiers: Black-Box Ownership Verification via Model Watermarking
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34942v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) offers efficient learning and inference for resource-constrained systems, yet ownership verification of its models remains underexplored. We present the first systematic investigation of model watermarking in HDC by adapting backdoor-based embedding to three classifiers with different prototype-learning mechanisms. Across four benchmarks, with conventional neural networks as references, we examine whether watermarks can be learned without compromising task accuracy and whether they survive subsequent model modification and replication. The error-driven classifiers, AdaptHD and OnlineHD, support verification at a nominal trigger exposure of 1% with at most 0.58 percentage points of mean accuracy loss, whereas single-pass Vanilla HDC requires greater exposure and can incur substantial accuracy costs. The error-driven models retain verification under native continued training, but extraction produces surrogates that reproduce much of the task behavior without verifiable watermarks. Watermark overwriting readily embeds attacker watermarks into HDC prototypes and erodes the owner's watermark more strongly than in the neural network references, although the strongest erosion coincides with large accuracy losses. We further deploy watermarked AdaptHD on an FPGA and stress its execution through undervolting and overclocking. Verification survives substantial computation errors, whereas more severe stress either causes verification failure together with accuracy collapse or results in inference timeouts. These findings establish the feasibility of watermarking in HDC while identifying limitations in retention under extraction and sensitivity to overwriting.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.34995v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study continuous-time stochastic linear--quadratic control with a scalar state and nonnegative control constraints. With quadratic running costs, randomized exploration can change the optimal mean feedback. We introduce an auxiliary problem without entropy in which the conditional policy mean is nonnegative and the covariance is prescribed in proportion to the squared state. Moment reduction and state separation yield two regional Riccati equations and characterize the finite-horizon value function and optimal conditional mean. We give a sufficient control--cost compatibility condition under which this mean coincides with the optimal feedback of the original constrained problem. For time-invariant coefficients, we characterize the undiscounted infinite-horizon optimum and establish mean square asymptotic stability under the stated assumptions. For unknown dynamics, we develop model-free actor--critic schemes for finite and infinite horizons. Numerical experiments compare the learned policies with their analytical targets and examine the effect of exploration on the optimal mean.

items.title: Macro Mondrian Conformal Risk Control
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35035v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conformal Risk Control (CRC) extends conformal prediction beyond the coverage setting to the control of general monotone loss functions, in a distribution-free and modelagnostic fashion. This makes it well-suited to problems with high-dimensional targets, such as the semantic segmentation task addressed in this work. However, CRC guarantees only marginal control, meaning that the risk is controlled on average over the data distribution. Under imbalanced distributions, the risk on inputs that contain rare objects may therefore remain uncontrolled, even when the marginal guarantee holds. We propose a new method that controls the risk on average over user-defined groups of the domain, drawing on Mondrian conformal prediction and macro-coverage algorithms. The method relies on a taxonomy, that is, a function that assigns a group to each data point, and reweights each point's risk by a coefficient that depends on its group probability, so that rare points contribute more than common ones. We illustrate the approach on two semantic segmentation datasets.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.35076v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Blendshape generation for 3D models has been extensively researched, but very few works address generating blendshapes for models with multiple disconnected parts. We present a case study of generating fixed facial expression blendshapes for commercial anime-style 3D character models with up to 11 parts per face. To make sure that our system can handle models in a way that is agnostic to topology, we train neural networks to generate deformation fields around the input meshes. We employ at least one network to independently process each part, and the relative positions of their outputs are coordinated by having each network also process the geometry of an anchor part. We use two mechanisms to improve accuracy: having the networks predict whether the output displacement is zero or not, and classifying blendshapes into different size groups and dedicating a network to each group. We also introduce a method to improve blendshape quality by enhancing bilateral symmetry. Our method is simpler than recent neural-network-based works and solves a real problem of the user community of these models.

items.title: Improving VLMs on Scientific Chart Analysis via Autonomous Evolution
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35077v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding and operating with scientific charts is a standard approach in data analysis, and while humans are good at interpreting such charts, open vision-language models (VLMs) are known to perform poorly when it comes to question answering based on such data types. Motivated by an initial observation that many of their errors are due to inexact answering, we raise the following natural question: how much accuracy can we recover without changing the model at all? In this paper, we study this question by searching over inference programs and the code around a "frozen" version of the model. Using ideas from autonomous evolution (famously used in AlphaEvolve), we first start from a baseline inference program, and in each round we show an LLM judge the code together with a few failures on training questions, and ask for an improving evolutionary move. As usual in autonomous evolution approaches, the candidate programs are kept in a small pool ranked by training accuracy, and the next edit is performed on top-scorers from this pool. We run this approach on three VLMs and four popular benchmarks on scientific charts, and we measure the fraction of descriptive questions whose answer exactly matches the ground truth. The accuracy improves in all experimental settings. On average, it rises from 16.6% with the starting program to 41.3% with the evolved one, and the largest single increase is 55.2 percentage points. As a side benefit, our evolved program is 3.8x faster than the starting program, because short answers are easier to grade and faster to generate. Our results demonstrate that a large part of the observed errors arise due to the inference pipeline, and that optimizing it can improve the "frozen" VLM without the need to retrain it.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.35092v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF) analysis according to ISO 21448, a machine learning object detector for light detection and ranging (LiDAR) point clouds can meet a performance target, a limit on the mean per-frame share of wrong detections among accepted detections, by rejecting detections above an uncertainty threshold. A threshold selected on data of one condition carries a statistical guarantee only for data distributed like its selection data, whereas SOTIF analysis covers every triggering condition. This paper presents an uncertainty evaluation in which the threshold is transferred into a triggering condition, a test decides at a stated error probability whether the target is applicable there, not applicable or not determined, and a lower bound counts the independent units an applicable outcome requires. For PointPillars ensembles on KITTI and nuScenes, counted in recorded sequences, as the dependence between frames requires, neither dataset held enough independent units for any target limit, and no transfer had a not applicable outcome. Counted in frames, the same data gave not applicable outcomes at limits fixed in advance after transfers into far distance, into rain and between two separately trained detectors, thresholds that met the target limit after a transfer rejected most correct detections, and in rain the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve did not decrease. A performance target met under one condition therefore counts as evidence under a triggering condition only after a test there, reported with its share of accepted correct detections and its number of independent recorded sequences.

items.title: Realizing Low-Precision Storage and Sparse Execution in a Folded FPGA Speech Enhancer
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35144v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hardware-aware training often optimizes FPGA resources, latency, or bit operations, but folding changes what compression saves: shared arithmetic decouples precision, weight storage, and scheduled work. We derive training objectives from the measured costs of a folded streaming speech-enhancement accelerator. Mixed-precision weights reduce on-chip storage; structured channel sparsity removes entire operations from the engine schedule. We deploy a bit-exact implementation on the Kria KV260. The best sparse model eliminates 47.3% of convolution MACs, cutting frame time by 45% (1.86 to 1.03 ms) and dynamic energy by 60% (83 to 33 $\mu$J/frame) against a storage-priced model measured in the same session, with higher speech quality. Relative to the most efficient dense build measured separately, frame time falls by 42% and energy by 48%. Reducing weight width from 8 to 6 bits lowers dynamic power by 27% but changes frame time by less than 5%. Plain channel group-lasso removes more work than cycle-cost-weighted lasso. Thus, folded-accelerator training should price storage and removable work separately, rather than rely on a single bit-operation metric.

items.title: Sequential versus fully conditional specification for tree-based synthesis of health data
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35163v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Disseminating synthetic data in place of original ones is a promising way to enforce privacy while complying with open science principles, especially in the healthcare domain. To keep pace with the rate at which researchers collect such data, there is a need for fast and flexible synthesis procedures. A popular class of such procedures is based on models of conditional distributions induced by decision trees. Such models can be combined into a synthetic distribution following two main approaches: sequential specification and fully conditional specification. However, there is currently no recommendation on which specification to use to optimize the risk-utility tradeoffs. In this work, we use both specifications to synthesize medical datasets by combining tree-based models of conditional distributions. We compare the quality of the resulting synthetic data using several metrics of risk and utility. Our results indicate no general superiority of either specification over the other. Sequential synthesis seems sensitive to the ordering of the variables, while the fully conditional specification involves more hyperparameters and incurs higher computational costs, which may limit its suitability for off-the-shelf synthesis procedures.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.35195v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop and analyze multilevel gradient-regularized Newton methods for unconstrained convex optimization with Lipschitz-continuous Hessians. By computing Newton corrections in lower-dimensional subspaces, the proposed methods aim to reduce computational costs while preserving the global $\mathcal{O}\left(k^{-2}\right)$ convergence rate in function values of the full-space method. To establish this rate for multilevel methods, we introduce a class of row-nested restriction operators that ensures monotonicity of the reduced-gradient norms across levels. Numerical experiments with row-nested operators demonstrate convergence behavior comparable to full-space gradient-regularized Newton, while offering substantial computational savings on large-scale instances.

items.title: mdRNAcat: A Molecular Dynamics RNA Catalog of REST2 Conformational Ensembles
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35204v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Learning molecular models of RNA requires simulation data that capture conformational variability and provide consistent physical training signals. Here, we introduce mdRNAcat, a curated dataset of all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of 48 RNA systems selected to promote sequence diversity. Each system is simulated using replica-exchange with solute scaling (REST2), with 32 Hamiltonian states and production lengths of 200-300 ns per state. The dataset provides atomic coordinates, instantaneous forces, and forces reevaluated under the unscaled reference Hamiltonian, together with structural annotations and replica-exchange metadata. Coordinates and forces are available at 1 ps intervals for the reference state and 100 ps intervals across all states in a standardized HDF5 format. We characterize conformational sampling, exchange behavior, base pairing, and sugar-pucker distributions to document the properties of the simulated ensembles. mdRNAcat provides a reusable resource for developing and evaluating data-driven RNA models, including coarse-grained force fields.

items.title: Identities, Not Pairs: Distribution-Free False-Accept Control for Embedding-Based Verification
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35277v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Embedding-based verification often calibrates a false-accept threshold from all impostor pairs among $m$ identities, although these pairs share identities. We characterize a worst-case limit: when hub identities score highly against a fraction $\rho$ of the population, a calibration-only threshold with marginal false-accept rate (FAR) at most $\alpha$ under every identity-exchangeable law reaches the hub score on hub-free calibration sets with probability at most $(m+2)\alpha/(2\rho)$. Uniformly accepting near that score at levels well below $\rho/m$ therefore requires trial information. We propose COVE, which ranks the trial pair among all $N=\binom{m+2}{2}$ pairs formed by augmenting the calibration units with the probe and reference. Under identity exchangeability, its marginal FAR is at most $\lfloor\alpha N\rfloor/N$, with first possible acceptance at $1/N=O(1/m^2)$. The rule also retains this guarantee with a fixed symmetric cohort-normalized score using an independent cohort. On 6 benchmarks and 8 frozen encoders, realised FAR was consistent with the exact bound. Where both valid calibration-only baselines accepted nothing, COVE retained a median $100\%$ of the sampled oracle's true-accept rate over reliable comparisons. In contrast, an empirical quantile over dependent pairs reached 2.87$\,\alpha$ FAR, and a binomial upper confidence bound over pairs missed its nominal 95\% conditional-FAR target in up to 55\% of calibration draws. Symmetric CSLS raised COVE's true-accept rate by up to 4.3-fold in the tested settings. The code is available in https://github.com/salimkhazem/Cove.git

items.title: Temporal-Difference Calibration of Black-Box Simulators
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35311v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a derivative-free temporal-difference (TD) framework for calibrating black-box simulators using one-step transitions from a target system and noisy simulator-generated continuation values. The calibration parameter is defined through Bellman orthogonality, recovering the physical parameter under correct simulator specification and yielding a near-optimal $L_2$ approximation of the policy value under misspecification. We propose three TD algorithms based on random-direction finite differences, distinguished by their query costs and reuse of noisy simulator evaluations. We establish almost-sure convergence, last-iterate mean-square error bounds, and central limit theorems for Polyak-Ruppert averages across four query-noise regimes. Our analysis reveals a specification-dependent bias phenomenon: for two algorithms, the finite-difference bias of the TD estimating equation vanishes at the calibration target under correct specification, even when the gradient surrogate remains biased. This permits a fixed perturbation radius and rate exponents approaching $1/2$ in the simulator rollout budget, whereas misspecification generally recovers the classical Kiefer-Wolfowitz rates. We also develop a few-replicate online bootstrap that yields Student-$t$ calibrated confidence intervals under negligible query noise, and identify a covariance mismatch that can invalidate conventional multiplier inference along Markov trajectories. Finally, a second-stage TD recursion corrects the remaining value discrepancy without additional simulator queries.

items.title: Beyond Wasserstein Proximity: Finding Better Transfer Sources
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35314v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Source selection often favors similar data, yet marginal proximity need not identify the most useful pretraining source. We motivate a conditional alternative through domain-adaptation theory and a regression example in which broader source variation improves estimation despite increasing Wasserstein distance. We examine five-day cryptocurrency volatility using ten Binance spot assets, six forecaster families, three seeds, and shared temporal cutoffs. Selecting the three farthest rather than nearest Gaussian-Wasserstein sources improves mean persistence-relative skill by 12.52 percentage points for MLP and 20.90 for Transformer, with positive post-hoc paired date-block intervals. Forward pilot selection improves mean skill over random transfer in all six families. Compact recurrent models achieve the lowest absolute mean errors, separating selection utility from forecasting quality. Retrospective five-candidate screening shows additional gains from farthest-first geometry before pilot ranking for MLP and Transformer. We distinguish across-target associations from within-target decisions and evaluate target heterogeneity, training seeds, and temporal-block sensitivity. Findings are exploratory for a fixed historical panel; the screening analysis measures no runtime saving.

items.title: One Megakernel is Not Enough: Predicting Where to Cut for Streaming Inference
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35336v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We address a fundamental question: How far should kernel fusion extend and which boundaries are worth preserving? Unlike the general convention of using one monolith megakernel at lower batch sizes or supporting only a selective model component as megakernel and rest of the model as conventional graph, we show that the best configuration is a composition of multiple megakernels with no overlapping conventional graph component, or a fully conventional graph. We present a framework that selects megakernel regions in a streaming inference model from conventional-graph profiles and standalone kernel benchmarks, without running any candidate design end to end. It simulates each candidate's tile and event graphs to predict time to first output and selects the measured best design in all 13 combinations of model and batch size we tested. Across NH-TTS, Qwen3-TTS and Llama-1B, the best composition ranges from two to four megakernels to fully conventional execution and none is a single megakernel. We introduce four model categories (megakernel-stable/ receding/ advancing/ averse) that capture how a model's best megakernel composition changes with batch size. Using NH-TTS model on H100 NVL GPU, we demonstrate that preserving three specialized megakernels can improve both latency and throughput despite introducing additional kernel boundaries. At batch size 32, this design delivers 21.4% lower mean batch-p95 time to first audio (TTFA) and 28% higher throughput than the evaluated monolith megakernel. Against conventional TensorRT graph execution, it reduces engine-level mean batch TTFA p95 by 4.05x and increases throughput by 19.7%.

items.title: Targeted Deep Regression - Initial Applications in Whole-Body Water-Fat MRI in UK Biobank
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35339v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: UK Biobank is a British clinical study which, in addition to large amounts of medical data collected, plans to include detailed Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) examina- tions from 100,000 participants. The image data can be analyzed for example by auto- mated analysis with neural networks for image segmentation or classification to expand the collection of image-derived phenotypes for medical research. In this work, we pro- pose, present and evaluate a methodology that uses image-based regression to estimate numerical properties from the collected neck-to-knee water-fat MRI scans. It applies a ResNet50-style network to 2D multi-channel collages that represent targeted and study- specific anatomical sub-regions from the MRI scan. The targeted sub-region sampling is achieved by propagating manually defined subregions from a reference scan to the other >30,000 analyzed scans using image registration. The resulting collages can be compact while retaining high-resolution, for example by providing multiple slices of kidney tissue for a kidney volume regression network. This approach also enables group-wise saliency analysis that highlight image and anatomical regions used by the network for the pre- dictions. The method was applied for the regression endpoints of kidney volume, heart volume, and age. Predictive performance was found between R2 = 0.731-0.984 and the group-wise saliency maps were found to highlight medically relevant regions. We con- clude that the method can be used to standardize and restrict the information presented to a deep regression analysis pipeline, increasing information density and opening up a wide range of future medical inference studies.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.35411v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We measure the emotion geometry of six LLMs spanning Google's Gemma 2 family. Using an extraction pipeline established by Sofroniew et al. (2026) on Claude Sonnet 4.5 and replicated by Hollowell (2026) on Gemma 2 27B base, we compare emotion geometry across base and instruction-tuned variants of Gemma 2 2B, 9B, and 27B. First, all six model cells exhibit the core emotion geometry. A linear map fit between two cells places held-out emotions nearest their own vectors in the target model. Across all fifteen model pairs, fit in one direction each, this failed exactly once, and the median rank was 1 in every pair. Linear maps refit on cleaned embedding-table vectors recover every held-out emotion at rank 1 in all thirty ordered pairs. Second, scale spreads the geometry's variance across more directions without weakening its tie to valence. The leading component's share of variance falls from 31.6 percent (2B) to 29.8 (9B) to 26.7 (27B) in the base models and from 31.9 (2B) to 29.2 (9B) to 27.3 (27B) in the tuned ones, while its correlation with human valence ratings stays between .71 and .78 in all six models. Third, we project each emotion vector onto the output vocabulary and ask at what depth the vector's own emotion word enters the top 10,000 of the 256,000 tokens. In the 2B and 9B models the median emotion word is there from layer 0, while in the 27B models it begins near chance, stays outside the top 10,000 for half the network, and enters at layer 23 in one step. Fourth, tuning leaves every registered analysis-layer measure within its floor. At every size, valence correlation rises and arousal correlation falls by amounts within their floors, the latter against prediction. PC2's variance share also falls, with a pooled decrease significant after correction. Mid-late layer stability exceeds its floor and traces to base 27B's final layer. Code, data, and audit reports are released.

items.title: A knowledge-driven nonconvex square-root regularization framework for joint group sparsity and structured smoothness
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35428v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Structured sparse learning is a leading paradigm for high-dimensional data modeling, as it enables rigorous integration of domain-validated structural priors into the learning process. Among these priors, pre-defined grouped structure and piecewise smoothness are ubiquitous in real-world applications. However, most existing structured regularization methods are built on squared loss and convex penalties, rarely jointly model these two complementary structural priors, and suffer from two key limitations. Their optimal tuning parameters are sensitive to the unknown noise level $\sigma$ due to the squared loss. Meanwhile, convex penalties induce inherent estimation bias and severe over-shrinkage of large magnitudes. To address these issues, we propose a knowledge-driven Nonconvex Structured Smooth Adjustment for Square-Root Regularization (NS$^3$R), which unifies the $\sigma$-free square-root loss with a joint nonconvex $\ell_{2,q}$ penalty ($0 < q < 1$) to simultaneously encode group sparsity and structured smoothness priors. Theoretically, we establish rigorous non-asymptotic error bounds for the NS$^3$R estimator under a mild $(2,q)$-group restricted compatibility condition. Computationally, we develop an efficient double-screened IRLS with thresholding (DS-IRLS-th) algorithm, which adopts a nested double-screening strategy to reduce computational cost and improve numerical stability, with provable global convergence for the resulting nonconvex optimization problem. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that NS$^3$R consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in finite-sample settings.

items.title: XL MIMO Extreme Learning Machines: Wave-Domain Inference with Stacked Metasurfaces
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35469v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The recently envisioned goal-oriented communications paradigm requires machine learning inference to be performed directly on wirelessly transferred data, by splitting neural network computations between the transmitter, the Receiver (RX), and the wireless channel. Such approaches aim to offload large portions of the computation onto the channel itself, which is often controlled by reconfigurable MetaSurfaces (MSs). Typical MS-parametrized systems, however, enable only limited computation offloading in the wave domain, usually corresponding to a single neural network layer, due to adverse channel fading effects and the almost linear operation of the channel and conventional MS models. In this paper, we demonstrate that an eXtremely Large (XL) Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) system equipped with Stacked Intelligent MSs (SIM) at the RX side, together with a single antenna and its accompanying radio-frequency chain, may act as a two-layer neural network operating exclusively over the air. The first (uncontrollable) network layer corresponds to the transformations offered by wireless fading, while the second (controllable) layer is implemented via SIM operations. In particular, only the first, front-end MS layer needs to exhibit nonlinear response to serve as an activation function. Leveraging the Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) framework, the proposed XL MIMO system architecture is shown to be a universal approximator, and the optimal linear-SIM-based combining is derived in closed form, allowing for fast training even and partial signal observability. Numerical evaluations across diverse datasets showcase that the proposed XL-MIMO-ELM framework achieves classification accuracy comparable to idealized digital models, thereby, proving the viability of low complexity, wave-domain neural computations.

items.title: FeatureLoop: Benchmarking Coding Agents under Evolving Requirements
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35488v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Software development with coding agents often begins with a rough request that users refine after trying the implementation. Final correctness alone does not capture the repeated guidance this process requires. We introduce FeatureLoop, a benchmark of 61 human-reviewed tasks from 34 repositories across five primary programming languages and seven software forms. Each task follows one development goal in a persistent workspace through evolution feedback, which adds or clarifies requirements, and completion feedback, which reports failures of stated requirements. Cumulative executable checks track new behavior, repair, and preservation of earlier functionality. We evaluate 12 frontier models and find that the strongest completes 72.1% of tasks with both feedback types. Across models, however, only 15.4% of observed failed stages recover within two corrective revisions. Further analysis reveals incomplete repairs, regressions, and model-specific differences in feedback use and token efficiency, identifying obstacles to reliable, low-intervention development.

items.title: Minimax Rates for Conditional Generative Learning under Wasserstein Loss
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35490v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study minimax rates for conditional generative learning under integrated Wasserstein loss, with H\"older continuous conditional laws and an unrestricted covariate distribution. We evaluate unrestricted generators through their conditional output distributions. For expected Wasserstein loss, the minimax rate agrees with the rate under uniform covariates and follows from balancing localization bias against unconditional distribution estimation error. Higher moments of the loss can instead be dominated by unobserved covariate regions, which force an additional risk contribution of order $n^{-1}$, where $n$ is the sample size. An adaptive localization argument gives matching upper bounds. The results cover unrestricted response laws and possibly vanishing Besov densities for $W_1$, and extend to higher Wasserstein orders under uniform response density bounds and integrability conditions. A multiscale lower bound closes the logarithmic gap in unconditional $W_1$ minimax rates in dimension two for both unrestricted distributions and Besov density classes. We also establish minimax rates for conditional Brenier maps under density, integrability, and uniform curvature conditions.

items.title: Query Complexity of Learning Axis-Aligned Partitions
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35495v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work establishes the query complexity of learning high-dimensional boxes in the exact query learning setting. Let $X \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a set of $n$ points, labeled by a collection of $k$ boxes: the label of each point in $X$ is determined by the unique box containing it. A learner aims to exactly recover the labels for every point in $X$ given access to a label oracle. We consider three increasingly-structured settings. In the most general setting, there are no conditions on the boxes, and they may overlap. We show that CAL (Cohn-Atlas-Ladner 1994), a classical active learning algorithm, is minimax-optimal with query complexity $\Theta(kd \log (n/kd))$. When the boxes are disjoint, we examine two regimes. In the large-$k$ regime, CAL remains minimax-optimal. For the constant-$k$ regime, an optimized variant of the Halving algorithm (Heged\"{u}s 1995) can beat CAL by a $\log(d)$ factor. Finally, in the most-structured settings, the boxes correspond to the leaves of a constant-sized decision tree. We prove a tight query complexity of $\Theta(d + \log n)$ that is additive in $d$ and $\log n$, generalizing a recent result (Black-Larsen-Mazumdar-Saha-So 2026) that establishes the query complexity of learning decision stumps.

items.title: Constraint Learning by Optimizing over Trained Neural Networks: A Pragmatic Tutorial
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35505v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Constraint learning is an emerging paradigm of modeling optimization problems with the help of machine learning. In this paradigm, trained machine learning models are embedded into the optimization model. For example, we can learn constraints empirically from available data, or we can avoid using a nonlinear objective function by learning a simpler approximation for it. Neural networks become a compelling option if the machine learning models must capture more elaborate and nuanced relationships. However, optimization models embedding neural networks may become too large or too slow to solve. In this tutorial, we present practical considerations for an effective and efficient use of constraint learning with neural networks and validate it with a case study highlighting the benefit of smaller and sparser networks.

items.title: Depth Improves Training-Time Scaling for Difficult Tasks in Deep Linear Networks
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35514v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural scaling laws describe the predictable power-law dependence of model performance on training time, dataset size, and model scale, with the exponents quantifying how performance changes with resources. Recent theory has shown how scaling exponents are shaped by the data distribution and the structure of the learning task, but whether network depth can improve training-time scaling has remained unsettled. Through a refined analysis of deep linear networks, we clarify that the task spectrum determines when increasing network depth improves training-time scaling. For spectrally difficult tasks, increasing depth improves the asymptotic training-time scaling exponent, whereas for easy tasks, the exponent remains independent of depth, with depth affecting only a logarithmic correction at the boundary between these regimes. Remarkably, we find that a reparameterization of time governed by the predictor norm provides a unified description of the dynamics across task difficulties. Under this reparameterization, the loss follows a common scaling law whose exponent is independent of depth. Numerical experiments on a task derived from benchmark image data and with nonlinear networks exhibit qualitatively consistent task-dependent effects of depth on training-time scaling. Our findings advance the theoretical understanding of how task structure shapes the effects of network architecture on learning and offer a basis for studying scaling behavior across broader classes of neural networks.

items.title: Explainable Prediction of High-Speed Solar Wind Streams driven by Coronal Holes via Topological Data Analysis
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35549v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: High-speed solar wind streams (HSSs) originating from coronal holes (CHs) are an important driver of recurrent geomagnetic activity. Since HSSs are associated to coronal structures visible in extreme-ultraviolet observations, this provides a natural basis for forecasting several days in advance. In this work, we investigate whether the topology of coronal structures observed in extreme ultraviolet (EUV) images contains predictive information on the subsequent occurrence of CH-driven HSSs at Earth. To this end, we consider Topological Data Analysis (TDA), and in particular persistent homology, to classify EUV solar images according to the occurrence of HSSs at Earth four days later. The target is a binary classification of HSS occurrence at a four-day lead time, defined using an HSS interval catalog and solar wind speed thresholds. Several combinations of topological representations and classifiers are evaluated under a common cross-validation framework. The results indicate that the topology of EUV coronal structures alone contains predictive information on subsequent CH-driven HSS occurrence, despite the absence of explicit CH geometric descriptors in the model input. To investigate the origin of this predictive information, we develop a model-level explainability framework based on cross-validation-aggregated feature weights and spatial evidence maps. A fully traced example connects persistence diagrams and persistence-image features to the classifier output and to their spatial localization in the original EUV observation. The proposed framework provides a transparent and computationally lightweight approach for investigating the relationship between coronal topology and subsequent high-speed solar wind streams.

items.title: Distributed Predictive Flocking for a Swarm of Miniature Vibration-Driven Robots in a Confined Arena
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35582v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coordinating many miniature robots in a confined arena, with no leader, central planner, or global map, is a core challenge for swarm robotics. As the swarm grows denser, collision avoidance becomes the limiting factor, and the number of safely coexisting robots depends on the formulation of the inter-robot safety constraint. We present a distributed predictive flocking controller in which each robot solves its own nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) problem, optimizing swarm cohesion and alignment costs, inter-robot and obstacle safety, and a task objective, while exchanging only predicted trajectories with local neighbors. Within this generalized controller architecture, solved in real time, we compare six barrier and control-barrier-function (CBF) safety formulations on a digital twin of an open-source vibration-driven bristlebot in a $0.64\,\mathrm{m^2}$ arena. A look-ahead discrete-time CBF performs best overall, with the fewest collisions and the widest inter-robot margins across nearly every swarm size tested. We deploy it on phototaxis, phototactic orbiting, and cohesion without a stimulus tasks, using swarm sizes starting from ten robots and up to the geometric packing limit. The swarm holds well: collisions stay low in small swarms, rising steeply as the packing limit approaches, while coordination and cohesion degrade gently rather than collapsing. The swarm is found not to trade safety for order, keeping both across the confined arena, with local alignment high at every swarm size.

items.title: Adversary Brains: Hypothesis-Based Logical Signatures for Threat Actor Detection with LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35624v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An adversary brain is an LLM-based model of a threat actor's behavior, held as an evolving logical signature: a hypothesis with enough structure that data can test it continuously, without a person re-interpreting it each time. Rather than any single observation, such as an IoC (Indicator of Compromise), it is the arrangement that becomes a detection, or intelligence, mechanism. Where YARA matches a file and Sigma matches a log line, an adversary brain matches the activity pattern of a campaign or threat actor. This is based on an intelligence analysis technique called Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (ACH), which the design lifts from the limitation of a few hypotheses at a time, to thousands, and then also operationalizes it for continuous detection purposes. Language models make the concept, and scale, practical: they turn prose reports into brains, judge matches, and drive the loop that keeps brains current. A partial pattern in a brain can also match a new value, such as a fresh C2 (command and control) domain name, assisting with the discovery of new indicators, and turning unknown unknowns into known unknowns, and potentially into knowns. The author would like to thank Ryan Moon for the collaboration, and Sounil Yu, Chris Inglis, Thomas Roccia, Marius Benthin, Israel Grimberg, Michal Kamensky, Justin Borland, Brandon Levene, John Hultquist, and John Bambenek for their feedback and assistance.

items.title: TRON: Transferring Naturally Evolved Network Architectures into Neuroevolution
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35647v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) is challenging because of the vast, non-linear space of artificial neural network (ANN) topologies. Evolutionary methods can generate architectures, but their effectiveness is limited by difficulties in preserving functional organization during mutation and recombination. Naturally evolved biological networks may provide organizational principles that support adaptation and evolvability. Here, we introduce TRON (TRansfer Of Natural networks), a neuroevolution framework that uses experimentally characterized protein-protein interaction (PPI) networks as architectural priors. Instead of starting from random topologies, TRON reuses biological interaction patterns as structural building blocks. It combines classical evolutionary operators with neuroevolution-inspired mechanisms, including speciation, and introduces species quarantine to protect newly generated architectures during early maturation. We evaluated TRON against established evolutionary and neuroevolutionary methods on three classification benchmarks (CORA, CITESEER, and PUBMED) and three regression benchmarks (DIABETES, FRIEDMAN, and CALIFORNIA). TRON achieved the highest predictive performance among the evaluated methods on all classification datasets and most regression tasks. It showed substantially lower variability across independent runs, indicating greater robustness and convergence stability, at increased computational cost. These findings support the use of PPI networks as effective architectural priors and suggest that biologically derived interaction networks provide more favorable substrates for neuroevolution than random topologies. More broadly, TRON demonstrates the feasibility of transferring naturally evolved network architectures into artificial intelligence systems, offering a direction for improving evolvability in NAS through the reuse of biological organizational principles.

items.title: Preference-Guided Cooperation in Multi-Objective Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35736v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-objective multi-agent reinforcement learning (MOMARL) addresses agent coordination and objective trade-offs simultaneously while optimising overall system performance. Existing work tends to treat multi-agent cooperation and multi-objective optimisation as largely independent components of a learning problem, which amounts to an exorbitant complexity except in trivial cases. We study here whether the structure provided by multiple objectives can itself be exploited to facilitate cooperation, rather than being treated as an additional optimisation challenge. We formulate MOMARL at both the team and individual levels and introduce objective-wise counterfactual credit assignment to evaluate each agent's contribution across the team objectives. We propose Meta-Gradient Informed Multi-Objective Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MIRL), with static (MIRL-S) and dynamic (MIRL-D) variants. By incorporating meta-gradient information, MIRL enables agents to learn how to prioritise objectives individually while collectively optimising the system-level objective, allowing the multi-objective structure to directly guide cooperation. Experiments on a multi-objective multiple particle environment show that our methods improve Pareto-front quality over baselines, with the dynamic variant achieving the strongest performance.
